Bury
bĕr´rĭ
v. (to place a body in the earth or a tomb; rendering Hebrew qabar, Greek thapto)
From Saxon byrgan, to hide or cover. The patriarchs bought fields to bury in, and the Apostle makes burial the very figure of baptism — so the word joins the hope of resurrection to a plot of ground.

Biblical Definition

To bury is to lay a body in the earth, and Scripture treats the act as a duty of love and a confession of hope. Abraham's first purchase in the promised land was a grave: “I am a stranger and a sojourner with you: give me a possession of a buryingplace with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight” (Genesis 23:4). A man who owned nothing else in Canaan owned a tomb, and it was an act of faith in the promise rather than a concession to death. The gospel itself is preached with a burial in the middle of it: Christ “was buried, and… he rose again the third day according to the scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4). The burial is not a detail between the cross and the empty tomb; it is the proof that He was truly dead, and it stands in the creed for that reason. From there the Apostle draws the believer's baptism: “Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). Burial is the picture immersion makes. Our Lord also subordinates the duty to Himself when the two collide: “Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22).

Webster 1828 Definition

To deposit a deceased body in the grave; to inter; to cover with earth; to hide or conceal. Scripture makes burial both an office of love toward the dead and the figure by which baptism preaches death and resurrection with Christ.

expand to see more

BURY, v.t. [Sax. byrgan, to hide, to bury.] To deposit a deceased person in the grave; to inter a corpse; to entomb.

2. To cover with earth, as seed sown.

3. To hide; to conceal; to overwhelm; to cover with anything.

4. To withdraw or conceal in retirement; as, to bury one's self in a cloister.

5. To commit to oblivion; to forget; as, to bury an injury.

BURIAL, n. The act of burying a deceased person; interment; sepulture.

Key Scripture

Genesis 23:4 — "I am a stranger and a sojourner with you: give me a possession of a buryingplace with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight."

1 Corinthians 15:4 — "And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:"

Romans 6:4 — "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life."

Matthew 8:22 — "But Jesus said unto him, Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead."

Modern Corruption

The funeral has been remade into a celebration that refuses to name death, and with the naming goes the resurrection hope that made Christian burial a confession rather than a disposal.

expand to see more

Christian burial was always a sermon. The body was treated with honour because it is the Lord's and will be raised; the grave was a bed rather than an end; and the words spoken over it named death plainly enough for the promise to answer it. Much modern practice has reversed both halves. The service is recast as a celebration of a life, death is not named, and the body — the thing Scripture says is sown in corruption and raised in incorruption — is often hurried out of sight beforehand so that nothing interrupts the tone. What is lost is not solemnity for its own sake but the occasion for hope, since a hope that answers nothing comforts no one.

Behind the practice lies a doctrinal drift: resurrection reduced to the survival of a soul or to a memory kept alive among the living. Scripture's burial language will not reduce. Abraham bought a field to bury in because he expected to receive the land; Christ was buried because He was genuinely dead; the believer is buried with Christ in baptism precisely so that he may walk in newness of life now and be raised bodily hereafter. Recover the plain confession, and the grave becomes what the fathers called it, a place of sleeping.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qabar (to bury) and qeber (grave, sepulchre) govern the patriarchal narratives; Greek thapto (to bury) and suntapto (to bury together with) give Romans 6:4 its force.

expand to see more

Hebrew qabar (H6912) — to bury; the verb of Genesis 23 and of the repeated notices that a man was buried with his fathers.

Hebrew qeber (H6913) — grave, sepulchre, burying place; the noun Abraham sought a possession of.

Greek thapto (G2290) — to bury; used in the gospel summary of 1 Corinthians 15:4.

Greek sunthapto (G4916) — to bury together with; the compound behind “buried with him by baptism” in Romans 6:4.

Greek mnemeion (G3419) — a tomb, sepulchre; the borrowed tomb from which our Lord rose.

Usage

"“That I may bury my dead out of my sight” — the first possession in the land of promise was a grave."

"“He was buried, and… he rose again the third day” — burial stands in the gospel summary as proof of real death."

"“Buried with him by baptism into death” — the ordinance pictures the burial it proclaims."
